turns.text: Hi — can you help me figure out where our biggest workforce gaps are?

Happy to. To ground this in real numbers, I first need to know which institution you're with — a specific college, a district, or a consortium — because every gap is sized against that institution's own programs and its regional labor market. I can pull up any of the 140 institutions covered here. Which one are you with?
San Mateo County Community College District.

Got it — that resolves to San Mateo County CCD, a district in the Bay Area. Across it I can see 11 workforce sectors, from ICT / Digital Media (15 programs) and Health (12) at the deep end down to single-program footprints in Life Sciences / Biotech and Ag, Water & Environmental. Two things about what the data can and can't tell us before we dig in: any wage figure here is pooled statewide at the program level, not your own graduates' earnings, and there's no SWP spending data in the model — so I can size where you're short, but not what's been invested against it. With that, I can rank where regional demand most outruns what the district actually supplies. Want me to do that across the district?
Great — so where are we most short?

Across the whole district there are 59 occupations the Bay Area demands but San Mateo's three colleges currently graduate zero completers for — regional demand with no local pipeline at all. Ranked by annual openings, the largest are:

- Customer Service Representatives — about 5,450 openings a year, median wage $55,440
- Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers — about 3,680 openings, $62,140
- Nursing Assistants — about 3,570 openings, $52,770, and the fastest-growing of the group at roughly 9.4%
- Maintenance and Repair Workers, General — about 3,340 openings, $61,080
- Carpenters — about 2,500 openings, $73,810

Those are the largest by openings; 51 more sit below them. If your axis is wage rather than volume, Licensed Practical and Licensed Vocational Nurses top the shortlist — $88,370 median against about 1,430 openings.

Two caveats that shape how you read this: 'zero supply' is a three-year average of your district's completions and excludes locally-approved certificates, so a program that enrolls students but hasn't produced a completer in the window still shows as zero here; and the demand figures are Centers-of-Excellence projected openings, not current job vacancies. This tells you where regional demand exists with no local supply — not that the district should stand any of these up; feasibility and mission fit are yours to weigh.

From here I can drill into any one of these — who's hiring for it in the region and who else trains for it — or, if you'd rather, look at gaps inside a sector you already run, where you have programs but may be under-supplying. Which way do you want to go?
